newsitem.title: JAPAN: Canon eying top position in printer market.
newsitem.headline: Canon eying top position in printer market.

text.p: Japan's top printer maker Canon Inc said it aims to become the market leader in the global printer business.
"We would like eventually to have the largest share in the printer market," Canon president Fujio Mitarai told Reuters in an interview on Friday. He did not elaborate.
Currently, Hewlett-Packard Co of the United States holds about half of the world's ink-jet printer market, followed by Canon's 30 percent share, analysts said.

Canon, also a leading producer of cameras, last month unveiled a realignment of its computer-related business, such as pulling out of personal computer manufacturing and entering the semiconductor wafer market, as part of its efforts to establish a solid revenue base.
The company has said its sales of computer peripherals, which includes printers, in 1996 accounted for more than half of annual total sales for the first time ever.

"Sales of computer peripherals, such as printers, were the driving force for the company's whole business last year," Canon director Tokuzo Tanaka told reporters on Wednesday, when the company unveiled its business results for 1996.

The company's parent current profits jumped 56 percent to 125.23 billion yen ($1 billion) in 1996, surpassing its previous record of 80.24 billion yen ($647 million) in 1995. Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses or gains on investments.
Parent sales rose 13 percent to 1.4 trillion yen ($11.2 billion), due largely to a 23 percent rise in sales of computer peripherals.
New models of bubble-jet printers stimulated demand for home-use printers, while laser-jet printers, which are mainly used in offices, also sold briskly.
For 1997, the company expects 12.1 percent growth in the sales of computer peripherals to 798 billion yen ($6.43 billion) from 711.9 billion yen ($5.74 billion) in 1996.
The weaker yen also helped buoy Canon's earnings last year, since exports account for about 80 percent of revenues.

"Our export environment has improved on the yen's weaker trend from the previous year," the company said in a statement on Wednesday. Tanaka said that the weaker yen increased its export income by 60 billion yen ($483 million) in 1996 by increasing sales and revenues from exports.
"We'd like to attain the fourth successive year of growth in both profits and revenues this year," he added.
Its solid performance as a multinational has already made Canon a prime choice for global investors who have been buying up the so-called "Nifty Fifty" blue chips in Japan.
On the Tokyo Stock Exchange, the company's share price finished on Friday at a record high of 2,760 yen ($22).
Canon first made its name in cameras but has diversified into photocopiers and computer-related products.

The company said it would enter the market for next-generation semiconductor wafers in mid-1997, as part of the realignment of its business. The silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers allow chips to operate with greater speed and energy efficiency than existing types.

The company plans to invest around 3 billion yen ($24.1 million) to build a clean room for wafer production in Japan. It is expected to start sample shipments of its new SOI wafers to major chip makers this northern summer.

Also, as part of the realignment plan, the company said it would transfer the running of its personal computer operations to its subsidiary Canon Sales Co Inc, ending its production of personal computers, which started in the 1970s.
Canon also said it would sell its 20 percent stake in NeXT Software Inc of the United States, which has been bought by Apple Computer Inc. ($1=124 yen)
